title: YOU LOVE JESUS… SO WHY DO YOU KEEP GOING BACK TO THE SIN YOU BEGGED HIM TO DELIVER YOU FROM?
paragraphs: YOU LOVE JESUS… SO WHY DO YOU KEEP GOING BACK TO THE SIN YOU BEGGED HIM TO DELIVER YOU FROM?
“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.” — Galatians 5:16
What if the battle you keep losing reveals something about how you have been fighting it? What walking by the Holy Spirit actually looks like when nobody is watching.
It happened again.
You promised God it would be the last time.

You prayed with tears running down your face. You deleted the messages. You walked away from the relationship. You closed the website. You surrendered the addiction. You promised yourself that tomorrow would be different.
And for a while, it was.
Then came the loneliness.
The temptation.
The anger you thought you had overcome. The memories you thought you had buried. The desires you thought had disappeared.
And suddenly, you found yourself standing in the very place you had begged God to rescue you from.
Now you're sitting there wondering…
How can I love Jesus and still struggle with this?
How can I worship on Sunday and fall apart on Monday?
How can I read Scripture, pray, and still feel drawn toward the things that are destroying me?
Perhaps the most painful part isn't even the failure itself.
It's the disappointment of becoming someone you promised God you would never become again.
But before you allow shame to convince you that there is no hope left, listen carefully to what the apostle Paul wrote:
“This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.” — Galatians 5:16 (KJV)
In the original Greek, Paul writes:
Λέγω δέ, πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς οὐ μὴ τελέσητε.
Legō de, pneumati peripateite kai epithymian sarkos ou mē telesēte.
A close translation would be:
“But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will certainly not carry out the desire of the flesh.”
There is something profoundly important hidden in the way Paul constructs this sentence.
The Greek word translated as “walk” is περιπατεῖτε (peripateite), from peripateō, meaning to walk, conduct oneself, or live one's life.
It is a present active imperative, communicating an ongoing pattern of living.
Paul is not describing a single emotional encounter with God.
He is describing a way of life.
Not merely what happens when the worship music begins.
Not what happens when the preacher lays hands on you.
Not the tears you shed during an altar call.
He is talking about how you live when the music stops, the church doors close, the emotions fade, and nobody is watching.
Because walking by the Spirit is not simply experiencing God's presence during worship.
It is living under God's direction in the ordinary, uncomfortable, and deeply personal moments of your life.
It is what happens when someone insults you and everything inside you wants to retaliate, but you choose restraint.
When someone betrays you and your flesh demands revenge, but you begin surrendering your bitterness to Christ.
When temptation appears on your phone at midnight and nobody would ever know what you chose, but you remember that your life belongs to Jesus.
When your pride wants to win an argument, but the Spirit leads you toward humility.
When your anxiety demands control, but you choose to bring your fears before God.
When your heart wants to return to something familiar, even though it was destroying you, but you choose obedience over temporary comfort.
Sometimes walking by the Spirit looks nothing like the dramatic spiritual experiences people celebrate online.
Sometimes it looks like quietly putting your phone down.
Apologizing first.
Walking away.
Telling the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
Refusing to entertain gossip.
Asking someone to pray for you.
Seeking help for an addiction.
Opening your Bible when your emotions tell you that God has abandoned you.
Sometimes the most significant spiritual victories happen in rooms where nobody applauds.
And heaven's work in your life may be far deeper than anything people can see.
Notice that Paul does not say, “Eliminate every fleshly desire, and then you will be qualified to walk by the Spirit.”
He says to walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh.
The order matters.

Many Christians spend their entire lives trying to become clean enough to approach God, when it is through Christ that they receive forgiveness and through the Spirit that they are empowered to live differently.
They are trying to defeat darkness while neglecting the light.
Trying to overcome sin through sheer determination.
Trying to manufacture holiness through guilt, fear, religious performance, and endless promises.
But Christianity is not merely a behavior modification program.
It is the transforming work of God in people who have been redeemed through Jesus Christ.
That does not mean discipline is unnecessary. Scripture repeatedly calls believers to obedience, self-control, vigilance, and resistance against temptation.
But Christian obedience is not independent self-reformation.
It is obedience empowered by the Holy Spirit.
Romans 8:13 declares:
“But if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.”
Notice those words.
Through the Spirit.
You are called to participate actively in putting sin to death, but you are not called to do it independently of God.
You cannot earn the Holy Spirit through your performance. According to Galatians 3:2–5, the Spirit is received through hearing with faith, not through works of the law.
You do not obey to purchase God's grace.
You obey because grace has reached you.
You do not fight sin to make Jesus love you.
You fight sin because the One who loved you and gave Himself for you is now calling you into a different life.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to confront an uncomfortable truth.
We have been asking God to remove temptations while deliberately keeping the doors to those temptations open.
We pray for purity while feeding lust.
We pray for peace while consuming endless outrage.
We pray for healing while repeatedly returning to destructive environments.
We pray for humility while secretly craving recognition.
We pray for deliverance while protecting the very habits that keep us enslaved.
We ask God to change our lives while refusing to surrender the things that are shaping them.
Paul addresses this principle in Galatians 6:7–8:
“Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
You cannot continually sow to the flesh and expect to reap the fruit of the Spirit.
What you repeatedly entertain matters.
What you normalize matters.
What you feed your imagination matters.
What you permit to influence your heart matters.
Not because one careless moment automatically separates a believer from Christ, but because the choices we repeatedly make have spiritual consequences.
And grace was never intended to become permission to cultivate the very sins from which Christ came to redeem us.
In Titus 2:11–12, Paul explains that the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives.
The same grace that forgives you also teaches you how to leave your old life behind.
But what exactly does Paul mean by “the flesh”?
The Greek word is σάρξ (sarx).
Depending on its context, sarx can refer to physical flesh, human existence, or humanity in its fallen orientation.
In Galatians 5, Paul uses it to describe human desires and ways of living that oppose the Spirit of God.
This does not mean your physical body is inherently evil.
God created the human body. Jesus Christ truly became flesh, as John 1:14 declares. Scripture even describes the believer's body as a temple of the Holy Spirit in 1 Corinthians 6:19.
The problem is not simply that you have a body.
The problem is sin's influence over human desires, attitudes, and actions.
And the flesh is not limited to sexual immorality.
Read Galatians 5:19–21 carefully.
Alongside sexual immorality, impurity, idolatry, and drunkenness, Paul identifies hostility, jealousy, fits of anger, selfish ambition, divisions, and envy.
That should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Because someone can avoid sexual immorality and still be consumed by pride.
Someone can preach against drunkenness while being addicted to attention.
Someone can publicly defend biblical truth while privately delighting in humiliating others.
Someone can know hundreds of Bible verses and still refuse to forgive.
Someone can look spiritually impressive while allowing bitterness, arrogance, and selfish ambition to govern their life.
The flesh can wear religious clothing.
It can speak Christian vocabulary.
It can quote Scripture.
It can stand behind a pulpit.
It can even disguise itself as righteous indignation when what it really wants is revenge.
And that is why walking by the Spirit cannot be measured merely by how religious someone appears.
Jesus said in Matthew 7:16:
“Ye shall know them by their fruits.”
Not merely by their platforms.
Not by their popularity.
Not by their spiritual vocabulary.
By their fruits.
Paul continues in Galatians 5:22–23:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.”
The Greek expression is ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματός (ho de karpos tou pneumatos) — “but the fruit of the Spirit.”
Interestingly, the word karpos, meaning fruit, appears in the singular.
Paul presents these qualities collectively as the fruit produced by the Spirit.
Love — ἀγάπη (agapē).
Joy — χαρά (chara).
Peace — εἰρήνη (eirēnē).
Patience — μακροθυμία (makrothymia).
Kindness — χρηστότης (chrēstotēs).
Goodness — ἀγαθωσύνη (agathōsynē).
Faithfulness — πίστις (pistis).
Gentleness — πραΰτης (prautēs).
Self-control — ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia).
These are not spiritual decorations designed to make Christians look impressive.
They describe the character that the Holy Spirit cultivates in the lives of believers.
And fruit takes time to grow.
A tree does not become mature because someone shouts at it.
Neither does spiritual maturity happen merely because someone has experienced a powerful emotional moment.
Growth involves abiding in Christ, receiving His Word, practicing obedience, enduring correction, repenting when we fail, and trusting God through seasons we do not understand.
Jesus explained this beautifully in John 15:5:
“He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.”
A branch does not produce fruit by declaring its independence from the vine.
It bears fruit through its connection to the vine.
In the same way, genuine Christian transformation is inseparable from our relationship with Jesus Christ.
This is why walking by the Spirit is not chasing spiritual experiences while neglecting Jesus.
The Holy Spirit glorifies Christ, as Jesus Himself teaches in John 16:14.
The Spirit will never lead you into something that contradicts God's revealed Word.
Not every strong emotion is the Holy Spirit.
Not every internal impression is divine instruction.
Not every opportunity is God's approval.
Not every uncomfortable conviction is condemnation.
We must test what we believe we are being led to do against Scripture, as instructed in 1 Thessalonians 5:21 and 1 John 4:1.
God's Spirit does not authorize what God's Word condemns.
And walking by the Spirit is not always comfortable.
Sometimes He confronts the attitude you have spent years defending.
Sometimes Scripture exposes the sin you renamed as a personality trait.
Sometimes obedience requires ending a relationship that continually draws you into sin.
Sometimes it requires confessing something that threatens your carefully constructed reputation.
Sometimes it means forgiving someone while maintaining necessary boundaries for your safety.
Sometimes it means accepting that you were wrong.
And sometimes the greatest evidence of spiritual growth is not that God has changed your circumstances, but that He is changing how you respond to them.
You no longer need to destroy someone to defend yourself.
You no longer need everybody's approval to know your worth.
You no longer need to pretend you are perfect to believe that Christ loves you.
You no longer confuse being offended with being persecuted.
You begin to recognize that surrendering your pride is more important than winning every argument.
That is transformation.
Not perfection.
Transformation.
And there is an important distinction between the two.
Galatians 5:17 acknowledges the conflict:
“For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other.”
Paul does not pretend that believers never experience temptation.
He acknowledges the opposition.
The presence of temptation does not automatically mean that you have been abandoned by God.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin, according to Hebrews 4:15.
Being tempted and consenting to sin are not the same thing.
But neither should the reality of spiritual struggle become an excuse for refusing to repent.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and deliberately making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and refusing to get up.
There is a difference between acknowledging your weakness and using your weakness to justify disobedience.
The Gospel does not tell us to celebrate our chains.
It tells us that Christ is our Redeemer.
And when you fall, the answer is not to hide from the One who can restore you.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Confession is not informing God about something He does not know.
It is coming out of hiding and agreeing with Him about what is wrong.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what you have done.
It involves turning away from sin and turning toward God.
You may cry without repenting.
You may regret the consequences without surrendering the behavior.
You may feel ashamed without actually wanting to change.
But genuine repentance brings us before Christ with an open heart.
“Lord, I have sinned. I cannot justify it anymore. Forgive me. Change me. Teach me to walk in Your ways.”
And when your repentance is sincere, do not allow your past to become an argument against the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is not permission to continue living in sin.
It is the assurance that those who are in Christ are no longer under condemnation.
Jesus did not endure the cross merely to give you another opportunity to hate yourself.
He bore our sins so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness, as 1 Peter 2:24 teaches.
Your shame cannot accomplish what His blood has already accomplished.
Your self-punishment cannot improve upon His sacrifice.
Your religious performance cannot purchase what His grace freely provides.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith, and the good works that follow are the result of His saving work in us (Ephesians 2:8–10).
This is the Gospel.
And this is why walking by the Spirit begins with dependence upon Jesus rather than confidence in yourself.
Tomorrow morning, before you reach for your phone, speak to God.
Not because a morning routine guarantees holiness, but because prayer expresses your dependence upon Him.
Read Scripture not merely to complete a religious obligation, but to allow God's truth to confront and shape your thinking.
When temptation comes, do not negotiate with it.
Remember 2 Timothy 2:22, which instructs believers to flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace alongside others who call upon the Lord.
Sometimes the spiritual answer is to leave the room.
Block the contact.
Install appropriate safeguards.
Seek accountability.
Speak with a trusted pastor, mature believer, or qualified professional when necessary.
Do not confuse practical safeguards with a lack of faith.
God can work through wise boundaries, Christian community, professional care, and the support of people who help you pursue healing and obedience.
And when you fail, return to Christ.
Do not wait until next Sunday.
Do not wait until you feel worthy.
Do not spend another month hiding behind a smile while your soul is quietly suffering.
Bring your sin into the light.
Receive correction.
Make necessary changes.
Repair the harm you have caused where possible.
And keep walking.
Paul writes in Galatians 5:25:
Here, the Greek verb is different.
στοιχῶμεν (stoichōmen), from stoicheō, carries the sense of walking in line with, following, or keeping in step with something.
Paul is calling believers whose spiritual life comes from the Spirit to bring their conduct into alignment with Him.
Keep in step.
What a beautiful picture.
You are not called to run ahead of God in self-confidence.
You are not called to deliberately resist His direction.
You are called to live in accordance with the Spirit who gives life.
One surrendered decision at a time.
One act of obedience at a time.
One honest confession at a time.
One difficult act of forgiveness at a time.
One moment of choosing Christ over the desires that once governed you.
There may come a day when you look back and realize that the things which once controlled your life no longer have the same hold over you.
Not because you became incapable of temptation.
Not because you became spiritually superior.
But because, through God's grace, you have been learning to walk differently.
The person who once responded with rage is learning patience.
The person who once lived for approval is learning contentment.
The person who once hid behind lies is learning honesty.
The person who once surrendered to every desire is learning self-control.
The person who once believed they were beyond redemption is discovering that the mercy of Jesus is greater than the darkness of their past.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not minimizing the damage.
Not rewriting sin as innocence.
But recognizing that through repentance, forgiveness, and the transforming power of Christ, your worst chapter does not have to define the remainder of your story.
Perhaps you are reading this with a battle nobody knows about.
Perhaps you are exhausted from pretending that everything is fine.
Perhaps you have been encouraging everyone else while secretly wondering whether you will ever experience freedom yourself.
You do not have to disclose the private details of your struggle to strangers.
Or simply write “I'm still fighting.”
Let it be an honest expression of your desire to surrender, not a performance for other people.
And when you see someone else commenting, remember that behind those few words may be a human being fighting a battle you cannot imagine.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Treat them with the gentleness you would hope to receive in your own weakest moment.
Someone in your family, your workplace, your church, or your circle of friends may be silently wrestling with the very things described here.
Your willingness to share biblical truth could help someone discover the courage to seek Christ, confess their struggles, and begin walking toward restoration.

Our desire is to continue expanding this work, making biblical resources available, reaching more hurting people, and creating Christ-centered content that speaks truth into a world increasingly desperate for hope.
That mission requires time, resources, dedication, and the generosity of people who believe in its purpose.
Scripture recognizes the importance of supporting Gospel ministry. Paul teaches in Galatians 6:6 that those who receive instruction in the Word should share good things with those who teach them.
And in 2 Corinthians 9:7, we are reminded:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
It can be part of how you steward the resources God has entrusted to you, alongside your other responsibilities and commitments to your local church.
If you have been looking for a meaningful way to support Christ-centered content and help biblical discipleship reach more lives, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
The Gospel must never become a privilege reserved for those who can afford it.
Before you leave, remember something.
Walking by the Spirit does not mean you will never hear the voice of temptation again.
It means temptation no longer has the rightful authority to govern your life.
You belong to Christ.
Galatians 5:24 reminds us that those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
The cross is not merely a symbol hanging around your neck.
It stands at the center of your redemption and your calling to a new life.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
And through faith in Him, you are called to walk in newness of life.
So when the old desires return, remember whose you are.
When shame brings up your past, remember the cross.
When your strength runs out, remember your dependence upon the Spirit.
When you stumble, repent and return to Christ.
When obedience hurts, remember that temporary pleasure is not worth surrendering to sin.
And when nobody is watching, remember that the God who sees your hidden struggles also sees every quiet act of surrender.
You may not yet be everything you desire to become.
But do not mistake unfinished growth for abandoned grace.
Keep abiding.
Keep repenting.
Keep trusting.
Keep walking.
Not in your own strength.
Not for the applause of people.
Not to earn the love of God.
But by the Spirit, through faith in Jesus Christ, for the glory of the One who gave Himself to redeem you.
The flesh may still remember the road back to your old life, but the Holy Spirit is teaching your feet to walk in a different direction.
